planting.note: Surface-sow or lightly cover seed in fall in a cold frame, or divide an established clump in spring, into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil under full tree canopy or dense shrub shade.

directions: A Japanese Asteraceae woodland perennial whose young, maple-leaf-shaped shoots are a classic spring sansai, usually boiled and served with sesame or soy. A true forest-floor plant, it needs humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in full tree canopy or dense shade and spreads readily by rhizome and self-seeding once established, so site it where that spread is welcome. Harvest young shoots in earliest spring before the leaves fully expand for the best flavor.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall for natural winter cold stratification, or divide an established clump in spring, into moist, fertile soil in sun to partial shade.

directions: Endemic to Ulleungdo Island, South Korea, where it is a traditional food and forage plant with a flavor between celery and lovage. It remains evergreen through winter in milder zones and is harvested fresh from autumn through spring, a rare winter-greens option for a partial-shade bed. Monocarpic flowering stalks die back after seeding while new basal foliage regenerates, so divide the clump or let it self-seed to maintain a continuous patch.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall for cold stratification, or divide an established clump, into deep, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil on a shaded bank or woodland floor.

directions: The Japanese counterpart to the North American sweet cicely species, this mountain-forest understory herb has anise-scented young leafstalks and roots eaten raw, cooked, or added to soups. It grows naturally on shaded stream banks and hillsides from lowland up to subalpine elevations, wanting deep, moisture-retentive, humus-rich soil. It is slow from seed, often taking more than a year to reach usable size, so most growers propagate by dividing an established clump instead.

subcategory: shade culinary and medicinal root herb

planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into deep, moist, fertile soil under high canopy; unlike most Apiaceae this species scorches in hot full sun and genuinely needs shade to part shade.

directions: A close Japanese relative of the already-present Chinese dong quai but a distinct cultivated species, grown commercially in Hokkaido and Nara for its aromatic root used in tea and tonic preparations, while its young leaves are also cooked as a vegetable. It is a true shade-to-part-shade forest plant and will scorch in hot full sun, so give it deep, moist, fertile soil under high canopy. Harvest roots in fall of the second or third year once the plant is well established.

planting.note: Direct-sow or root 20-25 cm stem cuttings after soil has warmed, staking or trellising for support, under tree canopy or shade cloth rather than open sun.

directions: A mucilaginous West and Central African potherb traditionally relay-cropped under cocoa or other tree canopy specifically because full sun makes the leaves thinner and harsher; shade-grown plants are preferred for soups and sauces, especially cooked with groundnuts and tomatoes. Pinch out flowering shoots to keep leaf production going through the season. It is closely related to the already-present Crassocephalum crepidioides but is a genuinely distinct species traded and eaten separately in Benin, Nigeria, and Cameroon markets.
sources: Genetic Resources and Crop Evolution (Springer) - Ethnobotanical investigation and diversity of Gbolo

planting.note: Root stem cuttings and train up a support or companion tree in dappled woodland shade or under 50 percent shade cloth; full-sun plants produce thinner, less palatable leaves.

directions: A rainforest understory liana from Central Africa, climbing from a tuberous rootstock, whose thick, dark-green leaves form the base of the eru dish, eaten raw or cooked in sauces. It genuinely needs shade cultivation rather than merely tolerating it, propagated almost exclusively from stem cuttings and trained up a support or companion tree under dappled canopy or shade cloth. The better-known sister species Gnetum africanum, already in the dataset, is a useful cultivation stand-in where this species is unavailable.
sources: PROTA (Plant Resources of Tropical Africa) - Gnetum buchholzianum
